Area Forecast Discussion
National Weather Service Baltimore MD/Washington DC
848 PM EDT Tue Aug 25 2026

.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
High clouds are plentiful as they drop down from the vicinity of
Lake Erie. It remains to be seen how much these impact more
optimal radiational cooling effects tonight.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
- 1) Strong thunderstorms are possible Thursday amidst
  increasingly warm and humid conditions.

- 2) After a brief cool down this weekend, hot weather will
  return next week.

&&

.DISCUSSION...
KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong thunderstorms are possible Thursday amidst
increasingly warm and humid conditions.

Any residual stratocumulus decks have dissipated with the loss
of daytime heating. However, high clouds continue to stream in
from the northwest which currently extend back toward Lake Erie.
Low humidity air sticks around through tonight. Surface high 
pressure will be nearly overhead, with light winds allowing low 
temperatures to drop to the mid 50s to mid 60s. Patchy fog is 
possible, especially west of the Blue Ridge, although the
mentioned passing high clouds may prevent full radiational 
cooling.

High pressure will depart off the coast Wednesday with surface
winds turning southerly. Some afternoon gusts up to 20 mph are 
possible depending on the degree of vertical mixing. High 
temperatures will tick up into the upper 80s to near 90, which 
comes with an increase in dew points/humidity levels. It looks 
like the atmosphere will remain capped most of the day, although
a pop up shower along the terrain could occur in the afternoon.
Moisture return increases overnight, which could result in some
scattered showers and storms. However, most of the 12Z guidance
has very limited to no coverage.

More notable forcing arrives Thursday as an upper level trough 
and surface cold front approach from the northwest. However, 
these forcing features may be somewhat displaced from the local 
area during peak diurnal heating. The front likely lags to the 
northwest while the strongest forcing with the trough passes to 
the north. A secondary shortwave may approach but not until the 
evening. Thus there remains some uncertainty in the coverage and
timing of any showers and thunderstorms. There is also some 
question on instability as there may be a fair amount of cloud 
cover around and perhaps some lingering morning showers. If 
everything were to come together though, moderate instability 
combined with shear of 20-30 kt could result in some strong to 
locally severe thunderstorms with damaging winds being the 
primary threat. Before and storms arrive, it will be warm and 
humid with highs in the mid 80s to near 90.

The cold front may bisect the area by Friday morning while the
mid/upper level trough axis remains to the west. Some showers
and thunderstorms will continue to be possible near and south of
the front, although the risk for strong thunderstorms is lower.


KEY MESSAGE 2...After a brief cool down this weekend, hot
weather will return next week.

The front may weaken or stall to the south this weekend while
high pressure builds eastward from the Great Lakes to St.
Lawrence Valley. Overall, the high should be strong enough to
shove most of the moisture to the south, although there is some
lingering potential for showers across southern areas on
Saturday. The coolest temperatures are also most likely
Saturday, with warming conditions expected Sunday as the high
pushes off to the east. Upper level ridging also builds eastward
on Sunday. Combined with return flow around the high, hotter
conditions are expected early next week with high temperatures 
rising back into the 90s by Monday for many locations. A 
diurnally driven shower or thunderstorm is possible, but the 
ridging should suppress most precipitation.

&&

.AVIATION /00Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH SUNDAY/...
VFR conditions are expected through this evening. Northwest
winds have begun to diminish post-sunset, becoming light and 
variable or calm tonight. Fog/BR is possible at MRB late 
tonight, but dense fog appears less likely at this time.

As high pressure pushes offshore Wednesday, southerly winds 
return for Wednesday with afternoon gusts up to 15 to 20 knots
possible. Some isolated to scattered showers may impact the 
terminals by Wednesday evening/night. 

A cold front will approach the region on Thursday. A few strong
to severe storms are possible that afternoon/evening, with 
gusty winds being the primary threat. As the front stalls nearby
Thursday night, some MVFR to IFR ceilings or visibilities may
develop.

Prevailing VFR conditions are expected on Friday and Saturday. 
Temporary drops to sub VFR conditions may be possible in 
thunderstorms on Friday. Light and variable winds are forecast for 
Friday. Winds shift out of the north to northeast on Saturday and 
are expected to remain light.

&&

.MARINE...
Winds remain light and variable tonight, with gusts generally 
topping out around 5 to perhaps 10 knots, before becoming 
southerly Wednesday as the high departs offshore. Winds may 
start increasing in the afternoon, but the greatest probability 
for 20 kt gusts will arrive Wednesday evening and night due to 
channeling. An advisory has been issued for many locations along
the Chesapeake.

With the next cold front not arriving until late Thursday, 
there are some hints of some 15 to 20 knot southerly gusts
continuing on Thursday. The front will also bring the risk of
strong, gusty thunderstorms, although these may not arrive until
late in the day.

Sub-small craft advisory level winds are expected on Friday as a 
cold front moves in from the north west. Special Marine Warning 
could be possible as Friday's thunderstorms move over the waters. 
Sub-SCA level north to northeasterly winds are forecast for
Saturday.

&&

.TIDES/COASTAL FLOODING...
Increasing southerly flow develops Wednesday into Wednesday
night, leading to rising water levels. Most locations will only
see action stages, but Annapolis could approach minor flood
stage early Thursday morning.
